2	\section{Introduction}
3	\label{sec:introduction}
4	
5	Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed for complex, long-horizon software engineering tasks---resolving GitHub issues, debugging production systems, and iterating on code across multiple rounds of edits \citep{jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent,wang2025openhands}.
6	As task complexity grows, a critical failure mode emerges that is qualitatively different from crashes or syntax errors: the agent \emph{stagnates}---continuing to produce actions that appear diverse on the surface while making no meaningful progress toward the task goal.
7	\citet{orlanski2026slopcodebench} systematically document this degradation in long-horizon coding tasks, finding structural erosion in 77\% of agent trajectories and verbosity increases in 75.5\%, with no agent fully solving any benchmark problem end-to-end.
8	Unlike overt loops, stagnation is insidious: the agent issues varied commands, edits different files, and generates plausible-looking outputs, yet its behavior is functionally stuck.
9	Detecting when an agent has entered this regime is essential for reliable deployment---enabling interventions such as early termination, strategy switching, or human escalation---yet identifying \emph{what signals} carry stagnation information, and whether complex language understanding is necessary to extract them, remains an open question.

12	\emph{Repetition detectors} identify exact or near-exact loops in action sequences, catching the simplest failure mode but missing semantically diverse stagnation where the agent varies its surface behavior while remaining functionally stuck.

% Abstract: Structural stagnation detection in LLM coding agents (EMNLP 2026 ARR)
\begin{abstract}
LLM agents deployed on long-horizon software engineering tasks frequently \emph{stagnate}---producing diverse yet collectively unproductive action sequences that evade simple loop detectors.
Detecting this failure mode is critical for enabling timely interventions, yet it remains unclear what information is needed: does identifying subtle agent stagnation require semantic understanding, or do simpler structural patterns suffice?
We present a systematic empirical study addressing this question through weak supervision over trajectories of two architecturally distinct agents, SWE-Agent (54,809 windows, 28.5\% stagnation) and OpenHands (150,652 windows, 6.6\% stagnation).
Our central finding is that stagnation signals are fundamentally structural: 30 hand-crafted features---command repetition rates, file operation counts, edit distances---achieve 0.995 in-domain and 0.967 cross-agent macro-F1, surpassing a GRU embedding probe (0.906 in-domain, 0.751 with full fine-tuning) by up to 21.6 percentage points and an LLM-as-judge baseline (0.663) by 33.3 pp, while requiring no GPU and running in under 5\,ms per window.
This structural advantage is encoder-agnostic: three embedding backbones all yield probe F1 above 0.90.
We further characterize labeling function temporal dynamics, revealing agent-specific roles: command repetition leads stagnation by 1.87 steps on SWE-Agent but reverses to lagging on OpenHands, where removing it improves probe F1 by 17.6\,pp.
Despite these well-characterized temporal patterns, three temporal label models---time-varying weights, HMM, and lag-aware HMM---all fail to improve over majority vote, a negative result we trace to low inter-LF conflict in the current 3-function regime.
Our findings redirect agent monitoring from costly representation learning toward lightweight structural approaches.
\end{abstract}

% Conclusion: Structural stagnation detection in LLM coding agents (EMNLP 2026 ARR)
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a systematic empirical study of progress stagnation detection in LLM coding agents, comparing structural features, neural embedding probes, and LLM-as-judge approaches against silver labels generated via weak supervision.
Three findings emerge.

First, stagnation signals are fundamentally structural.
Thirty hand-crafted features achieve 0.9951 in-domain and 0.967 cross-agent macro-F1, decisively outperforming a GRU probe (+8.96\,pp in-domain) and an LLM judge (+33.3\,pp)---all without GPU and in under 5\,ms per window.
This result holds across three embedding encoders (Qwen3, BGE-M3, E5-large), each yielding probe F1 above 0.90, confirming that the structural advantage is independent of encoder choice.
The practical implication is immediate: real-time agent monitoring need not rely on expensive representation learning or LLM inference when lightweight structural features transfer across agent architectures with minimal degradation.

Second, labeling functions exhibit systematic but agent-specific temporal dynamics.
Command repetition leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps on SWE-Agent but reverses to a lagging role on OpenHands (+3.32 steps), where its 92.3\% firing rate and 71\% false positive rate corrupt silver labels---removing it improves fine-tuned probe F1 by 17.6\,pp.
This finding has methodological significance for weak supervision on sequential data: labeling functions validated on one domain can become adversarial on another, necessitating per-agent validation and the circular evaluation methodology we develop to surface such pathologies.

Third, temporal sophistication in label aggregation does not improve detection.
Three temporal label models---TWV, HMM, and lag-aware HMM---all fail to surpass majority vote, with TWV actually degrading downstream performance by 2.57\,pp.
This negative result constrains future research: in the low-conflict regime of 3 binary LFs (95.1\% agreement at conf${\geq}$2), temporal alignment introduces more noise than signal.

These results suggest several directions for future work.
Expanding the labeling function set beyond three functions could create the inter-LF conflict necessary for temporal aggregation to add value.
Extending evaluation to non-coding agent tasks (web browsing, data analysis, multi-agent collaboration) would test whether structural dominance generalizes beyond software engineering.
Most critically, evaluation against human-annotated ground truth---for which we have prepared a 650-window gold set with a validated annotation pipeline---will determine whether structural features detect \emph{real} stagnation or merely reconstruct labeling function outputs.
